title: BRCA1/2 genetic test
what: This blood or saliva test looks for inherited changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These changes raise the risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
why: If several relatives had breast, ovarian, prostate, or pancreatic cancer, if breast cancer appeared at a young age, or to help choose treatment.
duration: the blood draw usually takes 5 minutes; results usually come in 2 to 4 weeks
tell_doctor: Who in your family had cancer and at what age, on both sides
If a relative already had a gene change found. Bring their report
If you had a blood transfusion or a bone marrow transplant
Why you want the test: to check your risk or to choose treatment

prepare.title: Counseling
prepare.text: It is best to talk with a genetic counselor or geneticist before the test: what it can show and what to do with the result.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: You usually do not need to fast. Check with the lab.

prepare.title: Family
prepare.text: Make a list of relatives with cancer: who, what cancer, and at what age.

bring: The list of relatives with cancer
A relative's genetic report, if there is one
steps: You sit down, and the nurse ties a band on your arm
The skin is wiped with antiseptic
Blood is taken from a vein into one tube
Sometimes saliva is collected in a tube instead of blood
The sample is sent to a genetics lab
feel: A quick prick, like a normal blood test
Feeling anxious is common and normal. Ask your doctor questions
after: Results usually come in 2 to 4 weeks
It is best to go over the result with a genetic counselor or geneticist
If a change is found, the doctor will talk about checkups and ways to lower your risk, and relatives may be offered the test
If nothing is found, it does not guarantee you will not get cancer. Your doctor will say what checkups you need

faq.q: If a mutation is found, will I definitely get cancer?
faq.a: No. Your risk is higher than other people's, but it is not a sentence. There are checkups and steps that lower this risk.

faq.q: Do I need to repeat this test?
faq.a: Usually not. Your genes do not change during your life, so once is enough.
Sometimes, yes. Men can have BRCA changes too and pass them to children of either sex.

reminders.text: BRCA genetic test tomorrow. Bring the list of relatives with cancer and their reports, if any.
